facts.text: The eastern whipbird is native to the east coast of Australia, where its whip-crack song is a familiar sound in eastern forests.
facts.quote: The eastern whipbird (Psophodes olivaceus) is an insectivorous passerine bird native to the east coast of Australia. Its whip-crack song is a familiar sound in forests of eastern Australia.

facts.text: It is dark olive-green and black, with a distinctive white cheek patch, a black crest, and a long dark olive-green tail tipped with white.
facts.quote: it is dark olive-green and black in colour with a distinctive white cheek patch and a black crest.

facts.text: The whipbird is heard much more often than seen, being a generally shy bird of the eastern Australian bush.
facts.quote: The eastern whipbird is generally shy, and is heard much more often than seen.

facts.text: Its famous whip-crack call is usually a duet: the male produces the long note and whip crack, while the female delivers the following notes.
facts.quote: The call is usually a duet between the male and female, the male producing the long note and whip crack and female the following notes.

facts.text: Calls are most frequent in the early morning, with smaller peaks around noon and sunset.
facts.quote: Calls are most frequent in the early morning, though do occur through the day with small peaks at noon and sunset.

facts.text: Its call recordings have been used in films such as Bush Christmas (1983) and The Dark Crystal (1982).
facts.quote: The call samples have been used in many films such as: Bush Christmas (1983) and The Dark Crystal (1982).

facts.text: It is insectivorous, recovering insects from leaf litter on the forest floor.
facts.quote: The eastern whipbird is insectivorous, recovering insects from leaf litter on the forest floor.

facts.text: Whipbirds are monogamous and may raise several broods in an extended breeding season from late winter through spring.
facts.quote: Whipbirds are monogamous. Breeding occurs from late winter through spring; a loosely built bowl of twigs and sticks lined with softer material such as grasses, located in shrubs or trees less than 3–4 m (9.8–13.1 ft) above the ground. Several broods may occur in an extended breeding season.

facts.text: The female incubates the eggs and broods the nestlings, while the male helps feed and cares for the fledglings for 6 weeks after they leave the nest.
facts.quote: The female incubates the eggs and broods the nestlings, though the male helps feed and take a more active role in looking after fledglings for 6 weeks after leaving the nest.

facts.text: It lives in wet temperate forests, including rainforests and wet sclerophyll forests, generally near water, and may be threatened by urbanisation.
facts.quote: The eastern whipbird is found in wet temperate forests including both rainforests and wet sclerophyll forests, generally near water.
